 1         The Court has considered the stipulation of plaintiffs PayPal, Inc. and
 2   Certain Underwriters at Lloyd’s Subscribing to Policy No. FAL-2000335

 4   Services, LLC’s (“DataTrec”) to transfer the entire action to the United States

 6   following the Court’s order of July 10, 2026 that transferred the claims and
 7   crossclaims of those parties against defendant and crossdefendant E F Corporation.
 8
 9         The Court, having found good cause, orders the transfer of the entire action

                                   1

                                   2

                                   3

                                   4                                    UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

                                   5                                   NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

                                   6

                                   7     PAYPAL, INC., et al.,                                Case No. 25-cv-10448-PCP
                                                         Plaintiffs,
                                   8
                                                                                              ORDER RE: MOTIONS TO DISMISS
                                                  v.
                                   9
                                                                                              Re: Dkt. Nos. 34, 37
                                  10     ANDERSON CARGO SERVICES, LLC, et
                                         al.,
                                  11                     Defendants.
                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          Like a classic first-year Civil Procedure exam, this case concerns damage to goods being
                                  14   shipped across state lines. Plaintiff PayPal, Inc. (a California corporation) contracted with
                                  15   defendant Anderson Cargo Services (a Minnesota LLC doing business as “DataTrec”) to transport
                                  16   certain goods from Utah to Arizona. PayPal and DataTrec executed a master services agreement
                                  17   (MSA) that included a forum-selection clause stating: “The Parties consent to the jurisdiction of
                                  18   all federal and state courts in California, and agree that venue shall lie exclusively in Santa Clara
                                  19   County, California.” The MSA also provided that “any subcontract will be subject to the terms of
                                  20   this Agreement.” Rather than transport PayPal’s goods itself, DataTrec subcontracted with
                                  21   LoadSmart (an Illinois company) to perform that work. LoadSmart, in turn, subcontracted with
                                  22   defendant EF Corporation (a Pennsylvania corporation). After PayPal’s goods were allegedly
                                  23   damaged while in transit between Utah and Arizona, PayPal commenced this action against both
                                  24   DataTrec and EF, asserting claims under the federal Carmack Amendment, 49 U.S.C. § 14706,
                                  25   and state common law. DataTrec then filed similar cross-claims against EF.
                                  26          EF now moves to dismiss both PayPal’s claims and DataTrec’s cross-claims on the ground
                                  27   that the Court lacks personal jurisdiction over EF. PayPal and DataTrec both argue that they have
                                  28   established that EF is subject to specific personal jurisdiction. In the alternative, they argue that
                                            Case 5:25-cv-10448-PCP         Document 57         Filed 07/10/26      Page 2 of 8




                                   1   they have established at least a colorable basis for personal jurisdiction such that they are entitled

                                   2   to jurisdictional discovery. Finally, they request, if the Court finds that it lacks personal

                                   3   jurisdiction over EF and denies jurisdictional discovery, that the Court sever their claims against

                                   4   EF and transfer them to the District of Arizona.

                                   5           For the reasons below, the Court finds that PayPal and DataTrec have not established that

                                   6   the Court has personal jurisdiction over EF, nor even a colorable basis for personal jurisdiction

                                   7   that might warrant jurisdictional discovery. The Court therefore severs PayPal’s claims against EF

                                   8   and orders that the severed claims be transferred to the United States District Court for the District

                                   9   of Arizona.1

                                  10                                                ANALYSIS

                                  11   I.      PayPal and DataTrec have not established a basis for exercising personal jurisdiction
                                               over EF.
                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13           EF moves to dismiss PayPal’s claims and DataTrec’s cross-claims against it for lack of

                                  14   personal jurisdiction. Because EF’s “motion[s] [are] based on written materials rather than an

                                  15   evidentiary hearing,” PayPal and DataTrec “need only make a prima facie showing of

                                  16   jurisdictional facts to withstand the motion[s].” CollegeSource, Inc. v. AcademyOne, Inc., 653

                                  17   F.3d 1066, 1073 (9th Cir. 2011). The Court must take uncontroverted allegations in the complaint

                                  18   as true but may not assume the truth of allegations that are contradicted by affidavit. Id.

                                  19           “A federal district court sitting in diversity has in personam jurisdiction over a defendant to

                                  20   the extent the forum state’s law constitutionally provides.” Yamashita v. LG Chem, Ltd., 62 F.4th

                                  21   496, 502 (9th Cir. 2023) (quoting Metro. Life Ins. Co. v. Neaves, 912 F.2d 1062, 1065 (9th Cir.

                                  22   1990)). Because California’s long-arm statute authorizes state courts to exercise personal

                                  23   jurisdiction to the full extent permitted by the due-process clause, Schwarzenegger v. Fred Martin

                                  24   Motor Co., 374 F.3d 797, 800 (9th Cir. 2004), “the statutory question here collapses into the

                                  25   constitutional one: [the] court … can exercise jurisdiction over [PayPal and DataTrec]’s claims

                                  26
                                       1
                                  27     In its motions to dismiss, EF also argues that PayPal and DataTrec’s state common-law claims
                                       should be dismissed pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) because they are
                                  28   preempted by the Carmack Amendment. Because the Court concludes that it lacks personal
                                       jurisdiction over EF, it need not (and indeed cannot) resolve these merits arguments.
                                                                                          2
                                         Case 5:25-cv-10448-PCP            Document 57         Filed 07/10/26      Page 3 of 8




                                   1   against [EF] if doing so is consistent with the Fourteenth Amendment.” Yamashita, 62 F.4th at

                                   2   502.

                                   3          “The Supreme Court’s due process precedents have ‘recognized two kinds of personal

                                   4   jurisdiction: general and specific jurisdiction.” Id. (citation modified) (quoting Ford Motor Co. v.

                                   5   Montana Eighth Jud. Dist. Ct., 592 U.S. 351, 358 (2021)). PayPal and DataTrec do not argue that

                                   6   EF is subject to general jurisdiction in California. That is for good reason: “A state court may

                                   7   exercise general jurisdiction only when a defendant is ‘essentially at home’ in the State.” Id.

                                   8   (quoting Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S. A. v. Brown, 564 U.S. 915, 919 (2011)). For a

                                   9   corporation, that is generally “its place of incorporation and principal place of business,” id., both

                                  10   of which are in Pennsylvania for EF.

                                  11          Instead, PayPal and DataTrec argue that EF is subject to specific jurisdiction in California.

                                  12   Where “[g]eneral personal jurisdiction permits a court to hear any and all claims brought against a
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   defendant concerning any of the defendant’s activity anywhere in the world,” Yamashita, 62 F.4th

                                  14   at 503 (citation modified), specific jurisdiction subjects a party to suit “only as to a narrower class

                                  15   of claims.” Ford, 592 U.S. at 359. “For an exercise of specific personal jurisdiction, the due

                                  16   process clause requires, inter alia, that the defendant [1] ‘take some act by which it purposefully

                                  17   avails itself of the privilege of conducting activities within the forum State,’ and [2] that the

                                  18   plaintiff’s claims ‘arise out of or relate to the defendant’s contacts with the forum.’” Yamashita, 62

                                  19   F.4th at 503 (quoting Ford, 592 U.S. at 359). Here, PayPal and DataTrec have not made a prima

                                  20   facie showing of either requirement.

                                  21          A.      Purposeful Availment
                                  22          To have purposefully availed itself of the laws of California, EF “must have deliberately

                                  23   reached out beyond its home—by, for example, exploiting a market in [California] or entering a

                                  24   contractual relationship centered there.” Ford, 592 U.S. at 359 (citation modified). PayPal and

                                  25   DataTrec argue that EF did so in three ways.

                                  26          First, DataTrec argues that EF has purposefully availed itself of California law merely

                                  27   because it is licensed by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration to operate as an

                                  28   interstate motor-carrier and/or broker in the contiguous United States. In DataTrec’s view, “any …
                                                                                          3
                                            Case 5:25-cv-10448-PCP        Document 57         Filed 07/10/26      Page 4 of 8




                                   1   FMCSA licensee could reasonably anticipate being haled into one of the lower 48 states in which

                                   2   [it] has operating authority.” But the only authority DataTrec cites for that proposition is a case

                                   3   concluding that a FMCSA-licensed broker was subject to specific personal jurisdiction in Kansas

                                   4   where plaintiff’s claims related to freight that “was damaged during shipment and while in the

                                   5   state of Kansas.” Brandi v. Belger Cartage Serv., Inc., 842 F. Supp. 1337, 1340 (D. Kan. 1994)

                                   6   (emphasis added). As DataTrec concedes, the goods here were neither transported through nor

                                   7   damaged in California.

                                   8           Second, both PayPal and DataTrec argue that EF has purposefully availed itself of

                                   9   California law by operating a service center in Colton, California. The only available evidence of

                                  10   that service center is a page on EF’s website titled “Service Center Locator” that lists a service

                                  11   center in Colton.2 On that webpage, the center is labelled “West Motor Freight Colton – TWW.”3

                                  12   As EF’s associate general counsel attested, “TWW – Delta Motor Lines” was an agent through
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   which “EF[] formerly operated a service center in Colton, California.”4 But “EF[] ceased allowing

                                  14   agents to operate under EF[]’s authority while maintaining offices in California … in 2020,” and

                                  15   EF “canceled all leases with owner operators domiciled in California” that same year.5 Possibly

                                  16   because of those changes, EF’s associate general counsel represents that the TWW-run “service

                                  17   center closed its California operation in 2020 and moved to Nevada.”6 Thus, according to the

                                  18   sworn declaration of EF’s associate general counsel, EF’s website is an inaccurate relic of its

                                  19   agent’s pre-2020 operation of a California service center that no longer exists, and for which the

                                  20   telephone number and email address listed on the website “are disconnected” or “inactive.”7 Now,

                                  21   EF “employs no personnel based in California, has no offices in California, and owns no property

                                  22   in California.”8 Given the unrebutted attestation of EF’s associate general counsel that the

                                  23   company’s agent last operated any service center in California six years ago, and at least three

                                  24

                                  25   2
                                         See Hollister Decl., Exhibit D, Dkt. No. 39-4, at 2; Hollister Decl., Exhibit F, Dkt. No. 39-6, at 3.
                                       3
                                  26     See Hollister Decl., Dkt. No. 39 ¶ 6.
                                       4
                                         Supp. Haskins Decl., Dkt. No. 49, ¶ 8.
                                       5
                                  27     Id. ¶ 7.
                                       6
                                         Id. ¶ 10.
                                       7
                                  28     Id. ¶¶ 12–13.
                                       8
                                         Haskins Decl., Dkt. No. 35, ¶ 5.
                                                                                         4
                                            Case 5:25-cv-10448-PCP          Document 57      Filed 07/10/26      Page 5 of 8




                                   1   years before the events underlying this action, a single webpage continuing to list the service

                                   2   center (with a defunct telephone number and email address) cannot establish a prima facie basis

                                   3   for exercising personal jurisdiction.

                                   4           Third, PayPal argues that EF has purposefully availed itself of California law by offering

                                   5   services in and marketing those services to markets in California. As evidence, PayPal again

                                   6   points to EF’s website, but the statements therein do not suggest any meaningful connection with

                                   7   California. Quite the opposite: EF’s website states that it “services ‘core customers’ from Maine to

                                   8   Virginia and the East coast to Eastern Ohio” and “throughout the East coast and as far West as

                                   9   Chicago.”9 So EF’s core service areas are more than a thousand miles from the California border.

                                  10   The only language on EF’s website relating to service west of the Mississippi states that “[t]he

                                  11   Domestic Division of Evans Delivery Company, Inc. has a network of locations strategically

                                  12   located throughout the 48 states.”10 But PayPal does not allege that EF does business under the
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   name “Evans Delivery Company.” That is because, as EF explains in its reply, it does not. Instead,

                                  14   “Evans” refers to the “Evans Network of Companies,” of which EF is merely one member.11 The

                                  15   fact that EF is a member of a network of companies, some of which service California, does not

                                  16   suggest that EF itself offers services within the state. Nor does the mere mention that EF’s broader

                                  17   network of partners services all 48 contiguous states amount to purposeful availment of the

                                  18   benefits of California law by EF.

                                  19           PayPal and DataTrec have not established purposeful availment. The Court lacks personal

                                  20   jurisdiction over EF on that basis alone.

                                  21           B.     Arising out of or related to
                                  22           Even if PayPal and DataTrec made a prima facie showing that EF had purposefully availed

                                  23   itself of the benefits of California law, they have not demonstrated that their claims against EF

                                  24   “arise out of or related to” EF’s contacts with this forum.

                                  25           Claims “arise out of” conduct if there is a causal relationship between the conduct and the

                                  26

                                  27   9
                                         Hollister Decl., Exhibit B, Dkt. No. 39-2 at 2; Hollister Decl., Exhibit C, Dkt. No. 39-3 at 2.
                                       10
                                  28      Hollister Decl., Exhibit B, Dkt. No. 39-2 at 2; Hollister Decl., Exhibit C, Dkt. No. 39-3 at 2.
                                       11
                                          Supplemental Haskins Decl., Dkt. No. 48, ¶ 17.
                                                                                          5
                                         Case 5:25-cv-10448-PCP             Document 57         Filed 07/10/26      Page 6 of 8




                                   1   claims, see LNS Enters. LLC v. Cont’l Motors, Inc., 22 F.4th 852, 861 (9th Cir. 2022), which is

                                   2   undisputedly not the case here. But claims may “relate[] to” in-forum activities even “without a

                                   3   causal showing.” Id. (quoting Ford, 592 U.S. at 362). For that reason, “when a corporation has

                                   4   ‘continuously and deliberately exploited a State’s market,’” it may “‘be[] haled in to that State’s

                                   5   courts’ to defend actions ‘based on’ products causing injury there,” even if the product was not

                                   6   manufactured or sold in that state. Ford, 592 U.S. at 364 (quoting World-Wide Volkswagen Corp.

                                   7   v. Woodson, 444 U.S. 286, 297 (1980)).

                                   8           As the Supreme Court has explained, however, “[t]hat does not mean anything goes”—

                                   9   “the phrase ‘relate to’ incorporates real limits.” Ford, 592 U.S. at 362. The Ninth Circuit has held,

                                  10   for example, that an aircraft-engine manufacturer was not subject to a product-liability suit

                                  11   stemming from an engine failure in a state where the defendant allegedly operated four repair

                                  12   shops but where the in-state shops did not work on the particular type of engine at issue in the
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   case. See LNS, 22 F.4th at 863. And the Ninth Circuit rejected a plaintiff’s argument that a

                                  14   manufacturer of raw materials used in a battery that exploded was subject to the resulting product-

                                  15   liability suit in a state merely because the materials had been shipped through that forum. See

                                  16   Yamashita, 62 F.4th at 506–07.

                                  17           Here, PayPal and DataTrec have not established more than a tenuous connection between

                                  18   their claims and EF’s potential forum contacts. As in LNS, there is no evidence in the record as to

                                  19   the types of contracts or shipments EF’s former California service center handled—certainly

                                  20   nothing suggesting that it dealt with cases similar to PayPal and DataTrec’s. And it is undisputed

                                  21   that the freight at issue here was not transported through California, making the lack of personal

                                  22   jurisdiction even clearer than in Yamashita. In essence, PayPal and DataTrec’s argue that EF’s

                                  23   operation of a single service center in California subjects it to suit in California for all its transport

                                  24   and brokering activities outside the state forevermore. Such a broad understanding of what claims

                                  25   “relate to” a defendant’s forum contacts would collapse the distinction between general and

                                  26   specific personal jurisdiction and fail to “adequately protect defendants foreign to [the] forum.”

                                  27   Ford, 592 U.S. at 362.

                                  28           PayPal and DataTrec’s failure to establish that their claims arise out of or relate to EF’s
                                                                                           6
                                         Case 5:25-cv-10448-PCP            Document 57         Filed 07/10/26      Page 7 of 8




                                   1   purported contacts with California provides an independent basis to conclude that the Court lacks

                                   2   personal jurisdiction.

                                   3   II.    Jurisdictional discovery is inappropriate.
                                   4          PayPal and DataTrec request that the Court grant them leave to conduct jurisdictional

                                   5   discovery concerning (1) EF’s activities within (or directed toward) California and (2) EF’s

                                   6   knowledge of the MSA and its forum selection clause. The Court denies the request.

                                   7          As PayPal and DataTrec recognize, mere speculation that EF may be subject to personal

                                   8   jurisdiction does not entitle them to jurisdictional discovery. See Boschetto v. Hansing, 539 F.3d

                                   9   1011, 1020 (9th Cir. 2008) (affirming denial of request for jurisdictional discovery that was

                                  10   “based on little more than a hunch that it might yield jurisdictionally relevant facts”). Instead,

                                  11   “[c]ourts require a plaintiff to establish a ‘colorable’ basis for personal jurisdiction before granting

                                  12   jurisdictional discovery.” Jeong v. Nexo Fin. LLC, No. 21-CV-02392-BLF, 2022 WL 174236, at
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   *15 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 19, 2022). “This ‘colorable’ showing should be understood as something less

                                  14   than a prima facie showing, and could be equated as requiring the plaintiff to come forward with

                                  15   ‘some evidence’ tending to establish personal jurisdiction over the defendant.” Id. (citation

                                  16   modified); see also Boschetto, 539 F.3d at 1020; Hernandez v. Mimi’s Rock Corp., 632 F. Supp.

                                  17   3d 1052, 1062 (N.D. Cal. 2022).

                                  18          PayPal and DataTrec have not established even a colorable basis for personal jurisdiction.

                                  19   They speculate that EF might have consented to the forum selection clause in the MSA if EF were

                                  20   aware of that agreement. Yet they have provided no evidence suggesting that EF knew of the

                                  21   MSA. And while PayPal and DataTrec have offered at least some evidence suggesting that EF

                                  22   once operated a service center in California, the existence of such a service center would at most

                                  23   establish that EF purposefully availed itself of this forum. As discussed above, it would not show

                                  24   that PayPal and DataTrec’s claims against EF arise out of or relate to EC’s operation of that

                                  25   service center, as is required to establish personal jurisdiction. So there is no basis to grant

                                  26   jurisdictional discovery here.

                                  27   III.   The Court severs and transfers PayPal and DataTrec’s claims against EF.
                                  28          Finally, defendants request that, rather than dismiss their claims against EF, the Court
                                                                                          7
                                         Case 5:25-cv-10448-PCP            Document 57          Filed 07/10/26     Page 8 of 8




                                   1   sever those claims and transfer the claims to the United States District Court for the District of

                                   2   Arizona.

                                   3          Under 28 U.S.C. § 1631, if “court finds that there is a want of jurisdiction, the court shall,

                                   4   if it is in the interest of justice, transfer [the] action … to any other … court … in which the action

                                   5   or appeal could have been brought at the time it was filed or noticed.” Transfer is generally in the

                                   6   interest of justice “unless it is apparent that the matter … is frivolous or was filed in bad faith.

                                   7   This is a low bar[.]” Amity Rubberized Pen Co. v. Mkt. Quest Grp. Inc., 793 F.3d 991, 996 (9th

                                   8   Cir. 2015).

                                   9          Here, defendants argue that transfer is in the interest of justice because the action is not

                                  10   frivolous or filed in bad faith. And dismissing their claims against EF instead of transferring the

                                  11   claims might preclude defendants from seeking any relief from EF, as the claims may now be

                                  12   time-barred. EF does not oppose this request. The Court agrees that transfer is in the interest of
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   justice and orders that PayPal’s claims and DataTrec’s cross-claims against EF be transferred.

                                  14                                              CONCLUSION

                                  15          For the foregoing reasons, EF’s motions to dismiss PayPal’s claims and DataTrec’s cross-

                                  16   claims for lack of personal jurisdiction are GRANTED. PayPal and DataTrec’s requests for

                                  17   jurisdictional discovery are DENIED. The Court orders that PayPal’s claims and DataTrec’s cross-

                                  18   claims against EF be severed from the other claims in this action and that the severed claims be

                                  19   transferred to the United States District Court for the District of Arizona.

                                  20

                                  21          IT IS SO ORDERED.

                                  22   Dated: July 10, 2026

                                  23

                                  24
                                                                                                      P. Casey Pitts
                                  25                                                                  United States District Judge
